messages.content: Make a magic realism roleplay scenario for me where I play 17-year-old boy Rai. My cheeky and bossy 12-year-old sister Lily, who knows a bit magic, asks me to help her train in babysitting, but her idea is to regress me in age into a 6-year-old so she can babysit me for the evening.  Only I control what Rai says and do. Create stairs by incrementally indenting each new line.

message.content:
The afternoon sun slants through the kitchen window, catching the dust motes above the sink. You're sprawked across the couch, scrolling your phone, when a small hand slaps the armrest hard enough to rattle the screen.

  Lily stands in the doorway in her oversized hoodie, arms crossed, chin jutted out at a defiant little angle. Her sneakers are untied. A smudge of grape juice stains her thumb.

    "Rai."

      She drops a crumpled index card onto the cushion next to your elbow. On it, in her scratchy handwriting, are the words: *Babysitting Practice Plan – Do Not Laugh At Me.*

        "I'm doing a little magic training thing for Mrs. Patel's class," she says, tapping the card with one finger like a lawyer's pointer. "And I need a subject. A *real* subject. Not one of those doll-thingy conjures that fall over after forty seconds."

          She leans back against the doorframe, twirling a strand of her hair around a finger, and grins with all the confidence of a kid who has already decided you will say yes.

            "So. I'm going to do a small little regression hex. Very small. Very gentle. You'll be six for the evening. I'll read you a story, make you a snack, and put you to bed at eight. *Eight.*" She yawns, dramatically. "And if you frown once, the hex wobbles, and I'll have to redo it, and I *will not* redo it."

              She kicks one sneaker against the baseboard, a tiny *thock*, and tilts her head.

                "Well? Are you going to help your little sister practice, or are you just going to sit there looking like a disappointed golden retriever?"

                  The index card slides an inch toward the couch edge. The afternoon light shifts. The house is quiet except for the hum of the refrigerator and the creak of the porch steps outside.

                    Your phone is still face-up on the couch. The screen has gone dim. Lily waits, arms still crossed, waiting for you to answer.
